query: A Merchant's Birthday {A cloth merchant from the capital is sixty tonight and wants a room full of young people laughing at his stories.|The cloth merchant is back, a year older by his own count, and he remembers which stories you laughed at.|The merchant's birthday again. He has started inviting his rivals, so that they can watch him be adored.} The cake is shaped like one of his ships. Be the life of the party {You laugh, sing, and dance with his aunt. He tips like a man buying a ship. You get home with the dawn and a sore throat.|He tells the story about the storm off the southern coast again, and you gasp in the right place. The tip is heavy; so are your feet.|You toast him in front of his rivals and he nearly cries. The purse he presses on you is shaped, faintly, like a ship.} {You laugh a moment too late at the wrong story, and he notices. A thin tip, and a long walk home past the castle's lit windows.|You call his ship by his rival's ship's name. The room goes quiet. The landlady pays you off early.|His rivals are funnier than he is, and you show it. He doesn't forgive it, and the tip says so.} Keep the glasses full {You pour, smile and stay out of the stories. The pay is fair, and the floor is very hard.|You keep the glasses full and your mouth shut. The merchant never learns your name, which suits you.|You pour for him and his rivals alike. Nobody notices you, and you go home with honest money and sore feet.}
